mappings.note: Names the 8 cm Mohenjo-daro figurine as the Dancing Girl - recall of an excavated object, so LO-109. The pairing item that turns on its being BRONZE also cites LO-124.
The decline setting in around 1900 BCE; the closing date of the first-cities development, matching the 2600 BCE start item.
Names climate change or the drying Sarasvati as a cause of decline - a fact about the end of the Indus cities.
Three defining marks of a civilisation: government, urbanism and writing. The concept behind LO-113's first cities.

Why surplus agriculture is a precondition for cities - the link from farming to urban populations that LO-113 is built on. Not LO-122, whose occupations are those of present-day rural and urban India.
The civilisation's spread over the Indus and Sarasvati plains across modern India and Pakistan: the development (LO-113) set on India's river plains (LO-107).
Why 'Indus Valley Civilisation' is now thought too narrow - the sites reach well past that valley. A point about the extent of the first-cities development.
Asks what EVIDENCE shows Harappan care for water and cleanliness - bathrooms, drains, wells and reservoirs as excavated features (LO-109) proving a civic trait (LO-113).
How we KNOW what the Harappans ate: grain remains, bones and residue analysis. The item is about method, so LO-109 alone.
What the Harappans exported - beads, timber, gold, cotton. Goods leaving India for regions outside it, so LO-123.
What the seals were for, at short-answer length: an artefact interpretation (LO-109) about how the cities traded (LO-113).
Farming tools and their likely wooden construction, inferred from clay models (LO-109), telling us how the Harappans tilled (LO-113).
Evidence for sea trade - coastal settlement and the Lothal dockyard: contact beyond India (LO-123) resting on a located site (LO-110).
Why the script resists decipherment; a limitation of the surviving source material, which is LO-109's second clause.
Names two everyday objects found at the sites - mirrors, pots, weights, combs. Pure artefact recall, so LO-109.
B. B. Lal's 'mutual accommodation' read as relative social equity - a claim about how Harappan society worked, hence LO-113. The companion item that asks for the EVIDENCE also takes LO-109.
Dholavira's three zones and stone foundations set against the usual two-part plan: a town-planning contrast (LO-113) turning on one named site (LO-110).
Streets aligned to the cardinal directions - a deliberate town-planning choice in the first cities. Not LO-105, whose directions are a map skill, not a feature of an excavated street grid.
Defines civilisation and lists five markers with Indus examples - the fullest statement of the chapter's central development, so LO-113.
Town planning and what it implies about authority and governance; still the character of the first cities. Not LO-119, whose government is India's own, today.
Wells and covered drains at Mohenjo-daro against Dholavira's stone reservoirs - urban water engineering, mapped like the shorter water items.
The evidence for Harappan farming and diet (LO-109) AND how that surplus fed the cities (LO-113). The stem asks both, so both are cited.
Common seal features and what they imply about trade, identification and literacy - artefact reading (LO-109) yielding a claim about Harappan society (LO-113).
Rival readings of the Great Bath and why certainty is out of reach without a decipherable script: an explicit lesson in the limits of evidence (LO-109) about a city structure (LO-113).
Causes of the decline AND an evaluation of the evidence for each, including why warfare is ruled out; the development (LO-113) weighed against the record (LO-109).
The peacefulness claim argued from the ABSENCE of weapons and battle scenes - reasoning from negative evidence (LO-109) about Harappan society (LO-113).

Infers belief from the Priest King, mother-goddess figurines, animal motifs and the swastika: artefacts (LO-109) read for religious ideas of the ancient period (LO-125). This is the chapter's one genuinely religious-thought item.
How the fertile, silt-fed river plains and their routes let the civilisation rise - India's physical features (LO-107) as the ground of the first cities (LO-113).

Asks specifically what ARCHAEOLOGICAL evidence supports Lal's accommodation view - uniform brick quality, shared drains, no palaces. Evidence-led (LO-109) about Harappan society (LO-113), unlike the shorter item on the quote's meaning.
Case study identifying the civilisation from grid streets, uniform bricks, covered drains and seals - recognising the first-cities package (LO-113) from its material traces (LO-109).

Climate case: a dry spell from 2200 BCE set beside the abandonment of Sarasvati-basin cities, and whether that supports invasion. Decline of the Indus cities (LO-113) argued from dated evidence (LO-109).

Rakhigarhi figurines read as a possible mother goddess, a revered bull and a wheeled cart, with a sub-part on why figurines matter when the script cannot be read: artefact interpretation (LO-109) reaching religious ideas (LO-125).

A planner reading Mohenjo-daro's two towns, cardinal street grid and uniformly good housing for hierarchy, deliberate planning and equity - all town planning and society in the first cities, so LO-113 alone.
